source.title: Scaling Makes It Possible: How Large Models Master Impossible Languages
source.authors: Ya-Ning Jia; Chun-Hui Zhang; Chiyu Ma; Zhong-Yu Ouyang; Ivory Yang; S. Vosoughi

record.file_problem: Whole paper and supporting information are present. Minor OCR and formatting artifacts do not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model perplexity across model sizes on systematically perturbed BabyLM language data, extending scaling-performance observations to impossible-language settings. It does not fit or test the original scaling-law functions.
record.gate_note: Rows record the tabled test-set perplexities across model sizes, including natural-language controls. The paper also plots Llama3.2-3B perplexity over training steps (Fig. 3) and reports results for its Lipschitz-Optimizer (Table 4/Fig. 6); these do not test parameter/token/compute power laws, and the optimizer comparison is the study's own method. Layer masking and noise-injection results (Figs. 4–5) concern layer contributions and perturbation sensitivity, not the claim versions. Table 5's token and compute estimates are specifications, not measured scaling-law outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study measures perplexity after fine-tuning pretrained models on perturbed text. Its size comparisons establish descriptive trends, but do not evaluate power-law form, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictive relationships. Invoking scaling laws does not make these results a test of the specified versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors attribute improved impossible-language learning at larger scales to a shift toward semantic abstraction, with near-control performance especially for reverse and hop perturbations. Semantic completeness alone does not eliminate all gaps: deterministic shuffle conditions remain worse than controls. The authors describe their findings as extending or aligning with scaling laws, but report no power-law fits or predictive scaling tests.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes existing models on perturbed BabyLM data and measures test-set perplexity; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting and extrapolation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity and the gap from natural-language controls vary by model size and perturbation type. The reported size comparisons also span different model families and training histories.

fits_no_version.finding: Within Qwen2.5, increasing size from 0.5B to 14B lowers perplexity in every tabled condition: NoShuffle falls from 2.71 to 2.47 and NondeterministicShuffle from 3.62 to 3.44. Relative perturbation gaps need not shrink: the latter rises from 33.6% to 39.3%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger pretrained models fine-tuned on perturbed BabyLM text achieve lower test perplexity, while relative robustness gains depend on the perturbation.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 and Llama3.2 differ substantially in fine-tuned perplexity, but these comparisons also change model family and pretraining history.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The evaluated Llama3.2 models achieve lower perplexity than GPT-2 on natural and perturbed BabyLM text after fine-tuning.

record.problems: No power-law fits, exponents, or extrapolation tests are reported. Model families and their training histories differ, so the cross-family comparisons do not isolate parameter count. Table 5's token volumes are referred to official reports and compute is estimated using FLOPs ≈ 6ND; the study does not vary these independently. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's Llama3.2 (1B) entries (three controls and seven perturbation conditions) are omitted to stay within the 60-row limit while retaining the GPT-2 and Llama3.2 (3B) endpoints, all Table 3 size conditions, and their controls. See Results B, Table 2.

untested.parts: Power-law scaling of held-out pretraining loss with parameters, tokens or compute under non-bottleneck conditions over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from laws fitted on small runs.
Loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute and its scaling exponents.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in fine-tuning or other modalities and training regimes; fine-tuning is performed, but this form is not evaluated.
A predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss; descriptive fine-tuning perplexity comparisons do not establish this.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The tabulated values and baselines are transcribed correctly. All row states become cannot_determine with respect to the specified versions; this does not mean the perplexities are unreadable or that size-related improvements are absent. Remove the V1 support verdict. Cross-family comparisons confound size with architecture, tokenizer and training history; even the within-family comparisons do not evaluate the claimed functional relationships. Table 5 contains reported training specifications and heuristic compute estimates, not independent scaling outcomes. The omitted Llama3.2-1B results are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares test-set perplexity across parameter scales on perturbed languages, but does not fit a power law or report exponents. It does not independently vary parameters, tokens and compute while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking; token and compute scaling are not tested.
No laws fitted on small runs are used to predict the losses of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No comparison holds parameter count fixed while varying depth, width or other architecture details.
The study fine-tunes models on perturbed text, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in fine-tuning or other training regimes.
No downstream-task performance or predictability from pretraining loss is evaluated.
The study does not compare fitting choices, report fitted exponents, or test whether curves bend away from a power law.

reader_labels.condition: Reported size series in Table 2 for GPT-2 and Llama3.2, and Table 3 for Qwen2.5; natural and perturbed language conditions
reader_labels.reason: Test-set perplexity is lower at larger listed sizes within the reported series. This supports a decreasing-with-size trend in these settings, but does not establish the claimed power-law form; rows r01–r60.
